notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:10

PURPOSE: Preserve depth for self-study without consuming live practice time.

LAND THIS: Generated reflection supports recall but does not prove skill.

SAY:
- This optional activity turns a course log into a study aid.
- A generated summary supports recall but does not prove that the learner can do the task.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “Part 4: Putting Prompts to Work”.

IF LATE: SKIP

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
THREE-MINUTE REP · PART 3
31
YOUR TURN — TURN YOUR COURSE LOG INTO A REPORT
One prompt, one keepsake report
3:00
STEP 1  ·  TYPE THIS → “List every prompt I have run in this course log, in order — one line each: what it did, and which element or move it taught.”
WHY → the log replays your whole course — every numbered prompt is in there.
STEP 2  ·  TYPE THIS → “Now turn that into my one-page course report: the seven elements with my own example for each, the loop, and the three prompts I will reuse at work. Anything the log doesn’t show: write UNKNOWN — don’t invent. Deliver the report, then stop.”
WHY → your examples, your report — with the Out and the Stop doing their jobs.
Both prompts are in tab EX-Report of your Course Workbook — run them in the course log you opened with Prompt 1.
Why this is the closing rep
Every numbered prompt you ran taught one move — and your log kept them all. The report writes itself because the raw material is real, yours, and already in the chat.

Step 1 opened the course by telling the AI to remember; this is the payoff. The report IS your first library entry: name it, date it, keep it.
Then compare with a neighbor: 
same course, different logs — which three prompts made THEIR reuse list, and why? Different fills, same anatomy.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) 3:00 badge. Frame the payoff: “your very first prompt today told the AI to remember everything — now you collect.” Both steps run in the SAME chat they have used all course (the course log).
2) STEP 1: the log lists every prompt it has seen, with what each taught. Let people scroll their own list — that quiet moment of “I did all that” is the point.
3) STEP 2: the one-page course report — seven elements with THEIR examples, the loop, and their three reuse prompts. Note the craft inside the prompt itself: it carries an Out (UNKNOWN, don’t invent) and a Stop (deliver, then stop) — the course’s own rules, applied to the course.
4) Neighbor compare: which three prompts made THEIR reuse list. Public commitment sticks.
5) Recovery (someone started a fresh chat mid-course, or their tool lost the thread): pair them with a neighbor’s log, or point at tab EX-Report — the numbered prompts are all there to rebuild from. The HANDOFF move from Part 1 is exactly the repair tool.
6) Skip only under extreme time pressure — this rep converts the course into an artifact they keep.

ACRONYMS —
none new on this slide.

CONTENT —
v1.12 (owner redesign): the rebuild-one-prompt rep is replaced by the COURSE-REPORT rep — “summarize all the prompts they’ve used through the course, so those informative examples give a full report.” Enabled by the new STEP 1 of Prompt 1/7 (the course-log acknowledgment). The old rebuild exercise (naive vs upgraded summary of the 60-word returns report) moved to tab EX-Report as a BONUS block for self-study; the symptom→element diagnosis grid stays at the top of the same tab.
The report doubles as Part 6 setup: it is literally their first library entry.
31

title: Optional extension: compare supplier quotations
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE
TIME: 0:00 (Optional self-study; no live allocation. The live course now runs the quotation work as two steps (slides 42-43); this page keeps the original one-step version.)
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:10

PURPOSE: Preserve depth for self-study without consuming live practice time.

LAND THIS: Quote comparison requires complete cost inputs or clearly marked gaps.

SAY:
- Quote comparison requires normalization of price, quantity, currency, and commercial scope.
- The three fictional quotation PDFs and workbook tab EX-Quotes ship in this package; run it as optional self-study.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “A deliverable needs artifact requirements”.

IF LATE: SKIP

MATERIALS: Quote_Alpha_Components.pdf, Quote_Bravo_Plastics.pdf, Quote_Cardinal_Metals.pdf + workbook tab EX-Quotes (all in the pack).

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 4 · WALKTHROUGH 1 · DATA
36
WALKTHROUGH · THREE QUOTES, ONE TABLE
Messy documents in, decision-ready table out
The input (also in your pack)
Three fictional supplier quotations (PDFs) answering the same RFQ — Alpha Components, Bravo Plastics, Cardinal Metals.
Deliberately NOT comparable at first glance: one quotes in euros per 1,000 units, one excludes tooling, one includes shipping, warranties differ 6–24 months.
What the room should notice: 
the “cheapest” quote stops looking cheapest once currency, per-1,000 pricing, tooling and freight are normalized — exactly the kind of buried-terms error AI is good at catching, IF you ask for normalization explicitly. The AI’s exchange rate must be flagged as an assumption to verify.
1
Extract & normalize
Extract every commercial term from these three quotations into one table: supplier, unit price, tooling, MOQ, lead time, payment terms, warranty, shipping terms, validity. Normalize prices to USD per unit at 5,000 units — state the EUR rate you use and flag it as an assumption — include tooling amortized over the 5,000 units, and note what shipping does and doesn’t include. Flag anything that is still not comparable.
2
Recommend, with caveats
Now: which quote has the lowest true landed cost at 5,000 units? Which is the best overall value once warranty, lead time and payment terms count? And what would you negotiate with each supplier before deciding? Keep it to one page; separate facts from judgment.
Works the same in a chat upload, Copilot, or your company assistant — this is G8 grown teeth. ✂ Both prompts: tab EX-Quotes of your Course Workbook.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Frame: “same discipline, messier input: three PDFs answering one RFQ — and they don’t line up on purpose.”
2) Name the traps out loud BEFORE running: Bravo quotes EUROS per 1,000 units and excludes tooling and freight (EXW); Alpha is straightforward but FOB; Cardinal looks priciest but includes shipping (DDP), waives tooling, and doubles the warranty.
3) Run STEP 1; check the table catches: per-1,000 → per-unit conversion, the flagged EUR assumption, tooling amortization, shipping inclusions.
4) STEP 2: the punchline — “cheapest” moves once terms are normalized; the negotiation question turns analysis into action.
5) Land the safety line: the exchange rate is an ASSUMPTION the AI must flag — and you must verify (house rule from Part 1).

BRIDGE —
“Analysis is answers. Next: turning answers into a file you can circulate.”

ACRONYMS —
RFQ = Request for Quotation. MOQ = Minimum Order Quantity.
EXW / FOB / DDP = shipping terms (Incoterms): EXW = buyer collects at the factory; FOB = seller loads, buyer ships; DDP = delivered to your dock, duties paid.

CONTENT —
Quote contents (answer key, from the generated PDFs): Alpha $13.90/u + $8,500 tooling, FOB, Net 30, 12-mo, 60-day validity · Bravo €11,900 per 1,000 (≈€11.90/u) + €14,000 tooling excluded, EXW, Net 60, 6-mo, 30-day validity · Cardinal $16.40/u, tooling waived, DDP, Net 45, 24-mo, 90-day validity.
At ~1.08 USD/EUR: Bravo ≈ $12.85/u + $3.02/u tooling ≈ $15.87 + freight; Alpha ≈ $15.60 + freight; Cardinal $16.40 all-in with double warranty — the ranking genuinely depends on freight and terms, which is the point.
36
